title: Bedrock bearer-token ("Bedrock API key") auth path is silently non-functional with the pinned boto3 version
intended_behavior: Per the module docstring (lines 8-16) and config.py's comment ("bearer token ... preferred over access key/secret"), setting only `bedrock_api_key` should let botocore's own token-provider chain pick up `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` from the environment automatically, with zero explicit wiring, and every Bedrock-backed AI call should authenticate with it.
actual_behavior: `backend/requirements.txt` pins `boto3==1.35.24`, which resolves a botocore release with no bearer-token support at all: I inspected the actually-installed botocore package (`.venv_test/Lib/site-packages/botocore`) and there are zero occurrences of `BEARER_TOKEN`/`bearer_token` anywhere in the source tree, and `botocore.credentials.EnvProvider` (the class that reads env vars into credentials) only recognizes `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`/`AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`/`AWS_SECURITY_TOKEN` -- there is no code path anywhere in this SDK version that ever reads `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`. `os.environ["AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK"] = bearer_token` at line 58 is therefore a complete no-op for authentication purposes with the dependency version actually shipped.
failure_scenario: An operator configures the Bedrock AI backend using only a bearer token (the documented/preferred, IAM-free method), leaving aws_access_key_id/aws_secret_access_key blank. `is_configured` returns True (`bool(bearer_token)`) so the UI reports it as configured. Every real `call_claude_json()` call then falls through boto3's entire default credential chain (none of which finds anything, since the only credential material given -- the bearer token -- lives in an env var this SDK never reads), and `self._client.converse(...)` raises `NoCredentialsError` (a `BotoCoreError`), which is caught at line 116 and re-raised as `RuntimeError(f"Bedrock invocation failed: {exc}")`. Every AI-backed analysis using Bedrock fails outright, with a confusing low-level "unable to locate credentials" message instead of any indication that the SDK version doesn't support the configured auth method.
proposed_fix: Bump boto3/botocore to a version that actually implements the Bedrock bearer-token/API-key feature, or stop relying on the undocumented-for-this-version auto env-var pickup and instead inject the bearer token explicitly (e.g. via a custom request-signing handler / `Authorization: Bearer` header registered on this client's own botocore event system), and add a startup/connection-test check that fails loudly if the installed SDK can't support the configured auth mode.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly. requirements.txt pins boto3==1.35.24 (no separate botocore pin); the resolved/installed botocore in backend/.venv_test is 1.35.99. A full-tree grep for 'BEARER_TOKEN'/'bearer_token' across that installed botocore package returns zero matches, and botocore.credentials.EnvProvider (lines 1089-1130) only maps AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY/AWS_SECURITY_TOKEN/AWS_SESSION_TOKEN -- there is no code path in this SDK version that reads AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK. In bedrock_client.py, line 58's os.environ["AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK"] = bearer_token is therefore inert for authentication with the pinned dependency version. Meanwhile is_configured (lines 50, 69-70) returns True purely from bool(bearer_token), so an operator who configures only the bearer token (the path config.py line 77 explicitly documents as 'preferred over access key/secret') gets a client that reports itself as configured but whose every real call() falls through the default credential chain, raises NoCredentialsError, and gets caught/rewrapped at line 116 into an opaque RuntimeError with no hint that the SDK version is the actual problem. This is not one of the documented intentional patterns (it's not graceful NOT_CONFIGURED degradation -- it actively misreports as configured then fails on every call), so it's a genuine functional/dependency-version bug. Severity: P1 is appropriate -- it fully disables one of two documented auth paths for a core AI integration with a misleading error and incorrect configured-status reporting, but the fallback IAM access-key/secret path still works and there's no security exposure or data loss, so P0 would overstate it.

title: _check_bedrock runs synchronous boto3 calls directly in an async function, blocking the whole event loop
intended_behavior: Like every other check in this file (all of which use `async with httpx.AsyncClient(...)`), _check_bedrock should perform its network I/O without blocking the FastAPI process's single asyncio event loop, so one admin's 'Test Connection' click can't stall every other concurrent request.
actual_behavior: `boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", **session_kwargs)` and `client.converse(...)` are plain synchronous, blocking calls invoked directly inside the `async def _check_bedrock`, with no `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` wrapper. This is the exact pattern the codebase's own production Bedrock client (app/ai/bedrock_client.py, `call_claude_json` -> `asyncio.to_thread(self._call_sync, ...)`) deliberately avoids for this exact reason. Here, the blocking network call runs directly on the event-loop thread.
failure_scenario: An admin (or the unauthenticated bootstrap-window caller, per _require_provider_manage_or_bootstrap) clicks 'Test Connection' for Bedrock against a slow, unreachable, or misconfigured region/endpoint. boto3's default connect/read timeouts can take many seconds to tens of seconds to expire. During that entire window, the single-threaded asyncio event loop cannot service ANY other request in the process -- every other user's IOC lookup, dashboard load, or API call served by that worker stalls until the Bedrock call returns or times out.
proposed_fix: Wrap the boto3 client construction and `.converse()` call in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`, matching the pattern already used in app/ai/bedrock_client.py.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading. `_check_bedrock` (connection_test.py, async def at line 374) calls `boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", **session_kwargs)` (line 400) and `client.converse(...)` (line 401) directly and synchronously with no `asyncio.to_thread` or executor wrapper, unlike every sibling backend check in the same file (_check_groq, _check_openai, _check_kimi, _check_deepseek, _check_xai, _check_mistral, _check_openrouter, _check_anthropic, _check_gemini, _check_ollama), all of which use `async with httpx.AsyncClient(...)` for non-blocking I/O.

Cross-checked the claimed contrast against app/ai/bedrock_client.py: its `call_claude_json` is `async def` and does `return await asyncio.to_thread(self._call_sync, ...)`, where `_call_sync` performs the actual `self._client.converse(...)` call. This proves the codebase already has an established, deliberate convention for keeping this exact blocking boto3 call off the event loop, and connection_test.py's _check_bedrock simply fails to follow it.

Traced the caller chain: test_ai_connection() dispatches to _check_bedrock via the handlers dict, and is awaited directly inside `ai_test_connection`, an `async def` FastAPI route handler in app/api/routes/ai_config.py (POST /ai-config/test). Since it's declared async def, FastAPI runs it on the single asyncio event loop, not in a threadpool (that special-casing is only for plain `def` handlers). So a slow/unreachable Bedrock region really would block that entire worker's event loop for boto3's default connect/read timeout duration, stalling every other concurrent request being served by that worker -- exactly the failure scenario described.

This isn't any of the 8 documented intentional patterns (not a status-mapping choice, not stale-role-claim handling, not graceful degradation, etc.) -- it's a genuine oversight: one check in an otherwise-consistent async I/O file breaks the non-blocking contract.

Severity: keeping P1 as claimed. It's a genuine availability bug matching the codebase's own precedent for why this must be threaded, but exposure is bounded -- the endpoint is gated behind provider:manage (admin-only) except for the narrow pre-first-user bootstrap window, and it's self-triggered (an admin testing their own possibly-misconfigured Bedrock credentials) rather than an externally exploitable DoS vector against arbitrary victims. That bounded-but-real impact profile fits P1 rather than escalating to P0 or dropping to P2.

title: max_requests / max_runtime_minutes / expires_at are collected and displayed but never enforced
intended_behavior: CreateAssessmentRequest (schemas/pentest.py:12-13) and AssessmentResponse (schemas/pentest.py:75-76) advertise max_runtime_minutes (1-1440 min) and max_requests (1-100000) as configurable hard caps on how long/how much an assessment may run -- pentest.py's create_assessment route persists them, and _serialize_assessment (pentest.py:86-103) echoes expires_at back to the caller as if it reflects a real deadline. PentestAssessmentStatus.EXPIRED exists and is explicitly checked as a halt condition in three separate places (orchestrator.py:373, exploit.py:296, and the add_target/scope comments), implying assessments are expected to actually reach that state.
actual_behavior: start_assessment (orchestrator.py:333-362) never computes or sets expires_at from started_at + max_runtime_minutes; _run_assessment (orchestrator.py:377-504) tracks request_count locally but never compares it against assessment.max_requests, and never checks elapsed wall-clock time against max_runtime_minutes anywhere in its per-target/per-tool loop. No other module in the backend (grepped for max_requests/max_runtime_minutes/EXPIRED/expires_at) ever sets expires_at or transitions any assessment to EXPIRED. The only way to stop a running assessment is a manual pause/cancel/emergency-stop or the global kill switch.
failure_scenario: A user creates an assessment via POST /pentest/assessments with max_runtime_minutes=5 and max_requests=10 (both accepted, both persisted, both shown back in the AssessmentResponse), adds many targets, and starts it. The assessment keeps scanning well past 5 minutes and well past 10 tool invocations -- the caps the API explicitly promised are silently no-ops, and nothing ever marks the assessment EXPIRED. For a tool whose entire purpose is to respect an authorized/bounded testing window, this is a real gap between the documented safety contract (visible directly in pentest.py's request/response schemas) and actual runtime behavior.
proposed_fix: In start_assessment, set expires_at = now + max_runtime_minutes; in _run_assessment's loop (and in _assessment_should_halt), check request_count >= assessment.max_requests and datetime.now(timezone.utc) >= assessment.expires_at, transitioning to EXPIRED and returning when either is hit.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading of orchestrator.py (lines 333-504 and the full file), schemas/pentest.py, and a full-backend grep for expires_at/max_requests/max_runtime_minutes/EXPIRED. start_assessment (349-353) and resume_assessment (540) never compute or set expires_at from max_runtime_minutes. _run_assessment tracks request_count locally (381, 447) but never compares it to assessment.max_requests anywhere in its loop. The sole halt-check, _assessment_should_halt (365-374), only checks the global kill switch, emergency_stopped, and status in (PAUSED, CANCELLED, EXPIRED) -- it never checks elapsed wall-clock time or request_count. A backend-wide grep confirms EXPIRED is only ever read (orchestrator.py:373, exploit.py:296), never written anywhere in the codebase, and expires_at is only ever read/serialized (routes/pentest.py:98), never set. schemas/pentest.py confirms these are real, documented, caller-facing API fields (CreateAssessmentRequest.max_runtime_minutes 1-1440, max_requests 1-100000, AssessmentResponse.expires_at). There is also no cap on total targets per assessment, so actual runtime/request volume is fully unbounded by the orchestrator and haltable only by manual pause/cancel/emergency-stop or the admin kill switch. test_pentest_api.py has no coverage of these fields' enforcement. This does not match any of the eight documented intentional design patterns -- it's a genuine gap between an advertised safety contract and runtime behavior. Severity: P1 is correct as claimed -- serious for a pentest tool whose safety model depends on bounded authorized-testing windows, but not an unauthorized-access/data-breach class P0 since it only affects the operator's own self-imposed limits and manual controls still work.

title: create_assessment applies none of update_scope's CIDR validation/size-cap protections to the initial scope_definition
intended_behavior: update_scope (pentest.py:179-225) was specifically hardened, per its own inline comment, to reject any single CIDR larger than a /16 and to reject non-syntactic CIDR strings, precisely so that 'the whole IPv4 Internet' can never become a valid declared scope for an assessment. Since scope_definition is the authorization boundary that gates every target add_target() will accept, this cap is meant to be a real safety/authorization control on the whole feature.
actual_behavior: create_assessment passes payload.scope_definition straight through to svc.create_assessment (orchestrator.py:200-236) with zero validation -- no CIDR syntax check, no size cap, nothing. CreateAssessmentRequest.scope_definition (schemas/pentest.py:11) is typed as a bare, fully permissive dict.
failure_scenario: Any user holding pentest:create (this includes the ANALYST role, not just ADMIN -- see models/user.py ROLE_PERMISSIONS) calls POST /pentest/assessments with scope_definition={"cidrs": ["0.0.0.0/0"]}. The assessment is created with that scope with no error, even though the exact same value submitted later via PUT .../scope would be rejected by update_scope's /16 cap. Every subsequent add_target() call for any IPv4 address (up to add_target's own /28 per-target cap) will now pass _is_in_scope() and be accepted as 'authorized', completely bypassing the very protection update_scope was hardened to enforce -- the protection only applies if the caller happens to use update_scope instead of just declaring the broad scope at creation.
proposed_fix: Factor the CIDR-syntax/size-cap validation out of update_scope into a shared helper and call it from create_assessment as well (or from svc.create_assessment itself so both entry points are covered by construction).

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against the actual source. `create_assessment` (pentest.py:128-143) passes `payload.scope_definition` straight to `svc.create_assessment` with no validation at all. `CreateAssessmentRequest.scope_definition` (schemas/pentest.py:11) is a bare `dict` with no Pydantic validator. `svc.create_assessment` (orchestrator.py:200-236) stores it verbatim: `scope_definition=scope_definition or {}` — no CIDR syntax check, no size cap.

By contrast, `update_scope` (pentest.py:179-225) explicitly validates every CIDR's syntax via `ipaddress.ip_network` and rejects any single CIDR bigger than a /16 (`_MAX_SCOPE_CIDR_ADDRESSES = 65536`), with an inline comment stating this exists specifically so "the whole IPv4 Internet" can never become a valid declared scope.

I confirmed the downstream authorization mechanism: `_is_in_scope` (orchestrator.py:120-139) accepts an IP/CIDR target if it is `subnet_of` any CIDR in `scope_definition["cidrs"]`. `add_target` only caps the size of the *target* being added (`_MAX_CIDR_ADDRESSES = 16`, i.e. /28), not the size of the scope CIDRs it's checked against. So if scope contains `0.0.0.0/0`, every single IPv4 address (a /32, trivially ≤ /28) is `subnet_of` it and passes `_is_in_scope` unconditionally — the entire scope-authorization boundary collapses to "allow anything."

I also confirmed `pentest:create` is granted to `Role.ANALYST`, not just `Role.ADMIN` (models/user.py ROLE_PERMISSIONS, lines 63-69), so this isn't an admin-only path — a non-admin analyst can call `POST /pentest/assessments` with `scope_definition={"cidrs": ["0.0.0.0/0"]}` and it is accepted with zero error, even though the identical value submitted via `PUT .../scope` on an existing assessment would be rejected by the /16 cap. This exactly matches the claimed failure scenario and is not one of the listed intentional design patterns (it does not resemble patterns 1-8; scan-flag restrictions (7) limit blast radius somewhat but do not touch the scope-authorization check itself, which is the actual control being bypassed).

Severity: the original reviewer's P1 is appropriate, not an over/understatement. This is a real bypass of a purpose-built authorization/safety control (the module's own docstring calls this "a standalone authorized-assessment workflow"), reachable by a non-admin role through the primary/default creation path (not an obscure edge case), and it fully defeats the scope-boundary guarantee for every subsequent add_target call. It stops short of P0 because: no destructive/exploit code path is unlocked by this alone (exploit execution remains gated separately by admin-only pentest:exploit per intentional design pattern 6), and nmap scans remain restricted to non-intrusive flags by a separate, unrelated safety boundary (pattern 7). So impact is bounded to unauthorized-scope active scanning/validation checks against arbitrary IPv4 hosts rather than arbitrary code execution — consistent with P1 rather than P0.

title: CIDR-typed scan targets skip the globally-routable-target check, allowing internal/private-network scanning
intended_behavior: Per the module's own comments (lines 284-292) and app/core/url_safety.py's assert_globally_routable_target docstring, the Security Assessment Toolkit is supposed to refuse to scan any target that resolves to a non-globally-routable address (RFC1918/link-local/etc.), specifically to prevent the toolkit's real subprocess/network tools from reaching this application's own internal docker-compose infrastructure -- exactly the 'http://opensearch:9200/...' SSRF the same comment says was found and fixed for IPv4/IPv6/DOMAIN/HOSTNAME/URL targets.
actual_behavior: In `_validate_scope`, the `if ioc_type == IOCType.CIDR:` branch (lines 260-275) only validates that the network is <=16 addresses (a /28); it never calls `assert_globally_routable_target` the way the `elif` branch for IPV4/IPV6/DOMAIN/HOSTNAME/URL does. The comment at lines 289-292 claims 'See url_safety.py's own docstrings for why this check does NOT apply to CIDR here' -- but url_safety.py contains no mention of CIDR anywhere (verified: zero matches for 'cidr' in that file), so the stated justification for the omission does not actually exist. nmap_tool.py (the only tool whose supported_types includes CIDR) likewise performs no independent routability check for CIDR targets, relying entirely on this function.
failure_scenario: An authenticated user with security_assessment:create permission creates an IOCLookup with ioc_type_hint='cidr' and ioc_value set to an internal range such as '172.19.0.0/28' (matching this deployment's own docker-compose bridge network) or any other RFC1918 /28-or-smaller block, then calls POST /security-assessment/run with tool_ids=['nmap_scan'], target_confirmation equal to that CIDR string, and authorization_confirmed=true. `_validate_scope` accepts it (network has exactly 16 addresses), and a real nmap subprocess is launched against the platform's own internal network, potentially port-scanning and fingerprinting the app's own Postgres/Redis/Neo4j/OpenSearch containers -- the same class of internal-reconnaissance result the file explicitly says was closed for single-host targets, left open here.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of backend/app/core/security_assessment.py, backend/app/core/url_safety.py, backend/app/security_assessment/nmap_tool.py, and the test suite. _validate_scope's `if ioc_type == IOCType.CIDR:` branch (lines 260-275) only enforces the /28 size cap via ipaddress.ip_network; it never calls assert_globally_routable_target, unlike the `elif` branch for IPV4/IPV6/DOMAIN/HOSTNAME/URL (lines 276-303) which does. The justifying comment at lines 289-292 ('See url_safety.py's own docstrings for why this check does NOT apply to CIDR here') is unsubstantiated -- I read url_safety.py in full and it contains zero mentions of CIDR; its only stated exemption is for the separate Pentest Suite (app/pentest/orchestrator.py), a genuinely different, correctly-scoped feature. nmap_tool.py -- the only tool whose supported_types includes IOCType.CIDR -- performs no independent routability check either; it only rejects targets starting with '-' (CWE-88 defense) and otherwise passes the CIDR string straight into asyncio.create_subprocess_exec([...,'nmap',...,target]).

The call chain is real and reachable by an ordinary authenticated user: app/ioc/detector.py auto-detects a bare string like '172.19.0.0/28' as IOCType.CIDR with no ioc_type_hint override even needed (lines 87-92), lookup.py's create-lookup route persists whatever type detect_ioc_type/ioc_type_hint returns with no value-matches-type check, and start_run's only gate before spawning the real nmap subprocess is _validate_scope.

Strong corroborating evidence this is an unintentional gap, not a deliberate design choice: (1) the test suite itself (test_security_assessment_service.py) asserts a private RFC1918 CIDR ('10.0.0.0/28') is ACCEPTED (test_accepts_a_small_cidr_at_exactly_the_cap) while a single private IPV4 host ('172.19.0.5') is explicitly REJECTED (test_rejects_private_rfc1918_ipv4_target) -- a direct, undocumented inconsistency in the same stated safety invariant; (2) the comment block at lines 79-85 of that same test file states the historical bug was that 'this function only ever format/destination-validated the CIDR IOC type -- IPV4/IPV6/DOMAIN/HOSTNAME/URL got none at all', and the visible fix only patched the latter group, leaving CIDR as the one type never brought up to the new routability standard; (3) docs/SECURITY_ASSESSMENT_TOOLKIT.md describes CIDR targets as capped-size but always 'the investigation's own already-detected seed IOC' (i.e., a real external target), with no documented exemption from the global-routability requirement. This is not one of the listed known-intentional patterns -- the Pentest Suite's RFC1918 exemption is a separate, correctly-scoped feature; this finding is about the Security Assessment Toolkit itself failing to apply its own stated invariant to one IOC type.

Severity: I concur with the reviewer's P1. Exploitation requires an authenticated user holding security_assessment:create (ANALYST/ADMIN tier) plus lookup:create, so it is not a pre-auth/anonymous SSRF, which caps it below P0. But it is a direct, easily-reproducible bypass of the exact security boundary this file dedicates significant code/comments/tests to enforcing for every other scannable IOC type, and it lets an already-authenticated but non-admin-required user launch a real subprocess-based nmap port/service scan (with CVE enrichment) against the application's own internal docker-compose infrastructure (Postgres/Redis/Neo4j/OpenSearch) -- the same class of internal-reconnaissance impact the file's own comments treat as warranting a dedicated UnsafeTargetError for single-host targets. That combination of low exploitation bar (ordinary product feature, no exotic conditions) and real internal-network reconnaissance impact, directly contradicting the module's own documented security guarantee, is consistent with P1.

title: correlate() assumes every relationship-extractor list element is a scalar, but crt.sh's `certificates` field is a list of dicts
actual_behavior: For each field in `_RELATIONSHIP_EXTRACTORS`, correlate() does `if not isinstance(values, (list, tuple, set)): values = [values]` and then, for each `raw_value`, builds the node/edge value as `str(raw_value)` (lines 126-130). The in-code comment (lines 120-122) explicitly assumes list elements are scalars ('e.g. VirusTotal's asn=15169 as an int'). However `app/providers/crtsh.py::_map()` (line 108-138) populates `data['certificates']` as a **list of dicts** (`{'issuer_name', 'common_name', 'name_value': [...], 'not_before', 'not_after', 'serial_number', 'id', 'entry_timestamp'}`), which is exactly the field this module maps via `('certificates', IOCType.TLS_CERTIFICATE, 'serves_certificate')`. No other producer of a `_RELATIONSHIP_EXTRACTORS` field returns dict elements (verified malwarebazaar, mitre_attack, otx, urlhaus, virustotal, whois_rdap all emit plain strings/ints for these fields) -- crt.sh's `certificates` is the sole outlier, and crt.sh is `requires_key=False`/`configured=True always`, so it runs on essentially every domain lookup.
intended_behavior: A TLS_CERTIFICATE node's `value`/node_id should be a clean, stable identifier for the certificate (e.g. serial number, fingerprint, or common_name) matching the 'DNS/network-topology fact' framing in docs/THREAT_INTELLIGENCE_GUIDE.md's confidence table, not a stringified Python dict.
failure_scenario: A domain lookup where crt.sh returns any certificate causes `str(raw_value)` on the full cert dict, e.g. producing a node/edge value like "{'issuer_name': \"Let's Encrypt\", 'common_name': 'example.com', 'name_value': ['example.com', 'www.example.com', ... dozens of SAN entries for a shared/CDN cert ...], 'not_before': '...', 'not_after': '...', 'serial_number': '...', 'id': 123456789, 'entry_timestamp': '...'}". This pollutes the frontend relationship graph and every evidence record built from it (app/evidence/builder.py's build_evidence_from_correlation), and for certs with many SAN entries the resulting string can exceed the 2048-char VARCHAR limit on `CorrelationEdgeRecord.target_value`/`source_value` and `EvidenceItem.related_ioc_value`, risking the exact uncaught StringDataRightTruncationError failure mode that ProviderResult.__post_init__ (app/providers/base.py) was specifically added to prevent for `source_url` -- but no equivalent guard exists for this path.
proposed_fix: Special-case dict-shaped elements when building the target value (e.g. pick a stable identifier such as `serial_number` or `common_name`/`issuer_name`), or have crtsh.py emit a flat list of certificate identifiers into `certificates` instead of full dict rows.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading both files directly. app/providers/crtsh.py::_map() (lines 108-138) builds data['certificates'] as a list of dicts (issuer_name, common_name, name_value list, not_before, not_after, serial_number, id, entry_timestamp), and CrtShProvider is requires_key=False/self.configured=True always, so it runs on virtually every domain lookup. app/correlation/engine.py::correlate() (lines 116-144) pulls this via _RELATIONSHIP_EXTRACTORS's ('certificates', IOCType.TLS_CERTIFICATE, 'serves_certificate') entry; since certificates is already a list, the isinstance(values, (list, tuple, set)) guard at line 120 does not wrap it, so each raw_value is one of these dicts, and line 127/129 does str(raw_value) directly on the dict to build both the GraphNode.value and (via _node_id) the node_id used as edge.target. I traced the full downstream chain: app/api/routes/lookup.py lines 179-192 splits edge.target on ':' and writes the resulting Python-dict-repr string straight into CorrelationEdgeRecord.target_value (app/models/lookup.py, String(2048)); app/evidence/builder.py's build_evidence_from_correlation (lines 124-140) does the same into EvidenceItem.related_ioc_value (app/models/evidence.py, String(2048)). No scalar-normalization or dict-specific handling exists anywhere in this path. app/providers/base.py's ProviderResult.__post_init__ (lines 85-96) confirms this codebase has already been bitten by exactly this failure mode once before for source_url ('uncaught StringDataRightTruncationError at insert time') and added a truncation guard there specifically -- no equivalent guard exists for target_value/source_value/related_ioc_value. The whole SSE lookup generator in lookup.py is wrapped in a single try/except Exception (lines 115...292-314), so a length-constraint violation wouldn't crash the process, but it would abort the entire in-progress lookup, mark it FAILED, and discard the already-computed correlation/evidence/final-assessment for that request -- worse in effect than a silently-swallowed error. Independent of whether any single cert's stringified dict exceeds 2048 chars, every domain lookup that gets any crt.sh certificate data already shows a garbage Python-dict-repr string as the TLS_CERTIFICATE node's value/id in the relationship graph and as EvidenceItem.related_ioc_value, directly contradicting the intended 'clean stable identifier' semantics documented via the confidence-table framing. Since crt.sh runs unconditionally on domain lookups, this is not an edge case -- it's the default path. This grounds a P1 rating: a core, always-on feature (relationship graph + evidence ledger) is functionally broken/corrupted for its most common producer, with a plausible secondary failure mode (full lookup failure) for certs with many SAN entries (common for CDN/shared-hosting certs). Not P0, since it doesn't compromise security/auth and doesn't corrupt data outside this one feature area.

title: Pre-run session_list() failure defaults the session baseline to {}, causing pre-existing unrelated MSF sessions to be misattributed to the current run
actual_behavior: If `client.session_list()` raises MsfRpcError before the module runs (lines 329-332), `sessions_before` is silently set to `{}` instead of aborting. After the run, `new_session_ids = set(sessions_after) - set(sessions_before)` (line 348) is computed against this faked-empty baseline, so any session that was already open on the msfrpcd daemon for an unrelated reason is treated as newly opened by this attempt.
failure_scenario: An earlier exploit attempt (against a different finding/target, or run by a different admin) left MSF session 3 open. A new run_module() call for a different finding hits a transient RPC hiccup on the pre-run session_list() call (falls back to {}), then runs a module that itself opens no session (e.g. mode='check', which never opens sessions by design). sessions_after still contains session 3 untouched; diffing against the faked empty baseline yields new_session_ids={3}, so the attempt is wrongly marked SESSION_OPENED with session_id=3, and finding_row.confidence/status get wrongly promoted to CONFIRMED/VALIDATED (lines 368-372) for a finding that this run never actually exploited.
proposed_fix: On a pre-run session_list() failure, fail the attempt outright (status=ERROR, no safe baseline to diff against) rather than substituting an empty dict.
