title: DROP/CREATE DATABASE and dump-replay errors are silently discarded, so a failed restore can be reported as successful
intended_behavior: Per the script's own docstring, stopping the writer services, terminating other connections, and dropping+recreating the database is supposed to guarantee a clean, empty database that the plain (no --clean) pg_dump output can be replayed into safely, and any failure in that sequence should be surfaced as a restore failure.
actual_behavior: `Invoke-DockerCompose "stop" ...` (line 101) pipes its return value to Out-Null, discarding the exit code. `pg_terminate_backend` (104-105), `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS $pgDb` (108) and `CREATE DATABASE $pgDb OWNER $pgUser` (109) are each run via `psql -c ...` with stderr sent to `2>$null` and stdout to `Out-Null`; `$LASTEXITCODE` is never inspected after any of the three. The replay itself (line 112) invokes psql without `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`, so per-statement failures during replay are not guaranteed to make the final exit code non-zero (psql's documented default behavior returns 0 as long as it 'finished normally', regardless of individual statement errors, unless ON_ERROR_STOP is set) -- and even that check (line 115) only ever covers the replay step, never DROP/CREATE.
failure_scenario: A stray connection to ioc_intel (e.g. an admin's own open psql session, or a reconnect racing the tiny window between pg_terminate_backend and DROP DATABASE) makes `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS ioc_intel;` fail with 'database is being accessed by other users.' That error is discarded. `CREATE DATABASE ioc_intel OWNER ioc;` then also fails ('already exists'), also discarded. The dump is then piped into psql (line 112) on top of the OLD, still-existing database; every CREATE TABLE/COPY collides with pre-existing objects and errors out, but because the dump's trailing statements (typically benign GRANT/ALTER/setval calls) can still succeed, psql can still exit 0. The script prints 'Restore complete. Restarting backend and celery...' and ultimately 'Restore complete and the backend is healthy' even though the database was never actually replaced with the backup's contents -- exactly the failure mode a disaster-recovery restore exists to prevent, occurring silently.
proposed_fix: Check $LASTEXITCODE immediately after the DROP and CREATE statements (and after the compose stop) and abort with a clear error before attempting the replay if any failed. Add -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 to the replay psql invocation so a failing statement both halts execution and yields a non-zero/well-defined exit code.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of C:/Users/User/ioc-intel-platform/windows/scripts/Restore-Database.ps1 (lines 100-113) and docker-compose.yml.

All specific technical claims check out:
- Line 101: `Invoke-DockerCompose "stop" ... | Out-Null` discards the return value. Notably, the SAME script checks this exact function's return value correctly elsewhere (lines 63-64: `$exitCode = Invoke-DockerCompose "up" "-d" "postgres"; if ($exitCode -ne 0) {...}`), and Common.ps1's own docstring for Invoke-DockerCompose (lines 173-186) explicitly documents that its return value is meant to be captured and checked. This makes the omission at line 101 clearly an inconsistency/oversight rather than intentional.
- Lines 104-105, 108, 109: each `psql -c ...` invocation sends stderr to `2>$null` and stdout to `Out-Null`, and `$LASTEXITCODE` is never read after any of them. Verified no `$ErrorActionPreference`/trap elsewhere in Common.ps1 or this script would catch a native-command failure here.
- Line 112: dump replay via `docker exec -i ... psql` with no `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` and no `--single-transaction`. Per PostgreSQL's own documented psql exit-code semantics, psql exits 0 if it "finished normally" (reached EOF) regardless of individual statement errors unless ON_ERROR_STOP is set (exit code 3 only triggers with ON_ERROR_STOP). So a dump replayed on top of a non-empty/stale database (e.g., because DROP/CREATE silently failed) can hit many "already exists"/constraint errors yet still exit 0.
- Line 113 correctly captures `$LASTEXITCODE` from the pipeline's last native command, and line 115 checks it — but this check only ever covers the replay step, never DROP/CREATE, exactly as claimed.
- Additional confirmation beyond the original finding: even when psql prints real per-statement errors during replay, they're merged into `$restoreOutput` via `2>&1`, but that variable is only ever printed in the failure branch (lines 116-119); the success branch (lines 125-140) never prints it, so genuine mid-replay errors are silently dropped from the user's view whenever the (unreliable) exit code happens to be 0.
- docker-compose.yml confirms only backend/celery_worker/celery_beat connect to Postgres from within the stack, so the "stray connection" vector is realistically an admin's own external psql session against the loopback-mapped host port (127.0.0.1:5433) — a plausible operational scenario during a disaster-recovery event, not a stretch.

This is a genuine error-handling gap in a destructive, admin-invoked disaster-recovery script: a failed DROP/CREATE or a partially-failed replay can be reported as "Restore complete and the backend is healthy" with no visible error, which is precisely the failure mode a restore script exists to prevent. It doesn't fit any of the eight known-intentional patterns.

Severity: P1 is appropriate and well-calibrated, not over- or under-stated. It's serious (silent success-reporting on a critical DR path, masking real data-loss/corruption) but it requires an explicit, elevated (`Assert-Elevated`), operator-confirmed (`-Force` or typed "RESTORE") invocation of a maintenance tool — not an attacker-reachable or default-path bug — so P0 (immediate critical/security) would overstate it; P1 (high-severity functional/error-handling defect with real operational impact) fits.

title: pg_dump's exit code is never checked, so a backup that fails partway through can still be reported as a successful, restorable snapshot
intended_behavior: A backup that pg_dump failed to complete should be treated as a failure, not retained as a valid snapshot.
actual_behavior: `docker.exe exec $containerName pg_dump -U $pgUser $pgDb 2>$null | Out-File -FilePath $dumpPath -Encoding utf8` (line 54) discards stderr and streams stdout straight to the dump file. The only success check (line 56) is 'file exists and length > 0' -- `$LASTEXITCODE`, which mirrors pg_dump's real exit status through docker exec, is never read anywhere in the script.
failure_scenario: pg_dump hits a permission error, a lock timeout, or a transient connection drop partway through a large dump, after several tables' COPY data has already streamed to stdout, and exits non-zero. The partial output already written makes $dumpPath non-empty, so line 56's check passes: 'Database backup written' is logged and the truncated/corrupt dump is kept in the 10-backup retention rotation (lines 62-65) as if it were a valid, restorable snapshot, silently degrading the platform's only backup safety net.
proposed_fix: Check $LASTEXITCODE immediately after line 54 and treat any non-zero value as a failure (route to the existing failure branch / delete the partial file), in addition to the existing empty-file check. Verified experimentally that $LASTEXITCODE correctly carries a failing native command's real exit code through a `| Out-File` pipeline even when partial output was already written before the failure.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading Backup-Database.ps1 directly. Line 54 pipes `docker.exe exec ... pg_dump ...` into `Out-File`; since Out-File is a cmdlet (not a native exe), $LASTEXITCODE after this line reflects docker.exe's exit code, which docker exec sets to the exit code of the process it ran in the container (pg_dump's real status) -- this is standard, well-documented PowerShell/docker behavior. Line 56 is the only success gate and checks solely file-exists + length>0; $LASTEXITCODE is never referenced anywhere in the script. If pg_dump fails after already streaming partial COPY data to stdout (permission error, lock timeout, container disk full, etc.), the partial file is non-empty, so the script logs 'Database backup written', keeps the truncated dump in the 10-backup rotation, and this is the only backup mechanism in the repo (no Restore-Database.ps1 or other verification exists) -- so corruption would only surface during an actual disaster-recovery restore. Common.ps1's own Invoke-DockerCompose shows the codebase author is normally meticulous about native-command exit-code/pipeline semantics, reinforcing that this omission in Backup-Database.ps1 is an oversight, not intentional. Does not match any of the eight documented intentional-pattern exclusions. Severity P1 is appropriate: silent corruption of the sole backup safety net with worst-case discovery during recovery, but not P0 since it requires a specific mid-dump failure trigger rather than affecting every backup unconditionally, and it's a reliability defect rather than a security vulnerability.

title: Unhandled Test-Path exception on ACL-locked config folder crashes the whole script, breaking the JSON-output contract
actual_behavior: Line 34 sets `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` for the whole script. Line 134 does `$existingInstall = Test-Path (Join-Path $dataDir "config\.env")` with no try/catch, where `$dataDir` is `ProgramData\IOC Intelligence Platform` -- a folder that Common.ps1's Initialize-DataDirectories locks down via `icacls /inheritance:r /grant:r` to Administrators+SYSTEM only once any prior install has run. I reproduced this live on this machine (which has a real prior install): running the script non-elevated produced `Test-Path : Access is denied ... At Check-Prerequisites.ps1:134` and the process exited with code 1 -- no JSON was ever written to stdout, and none of the checks after line 134 (which is only the last few lines, but crucially the exit-code/JSON contract itself) ran.
intended_behavior: Per its own docstring, this script must always 'emit one JSON object to stdout (and nothing else)' with exit code 0/1 reflecting real hard-check results, and is explicitly described as 'independently runnable by an administrator for diagnostics' (i.e., not guaranteed to be running with an elevated token, since being an admin account and having an elevated token are different things -- a distinction this same codebase's own Assert-Elevated function in Common.ps1 is built entirely around).
failure_scenario: Any administrator double-clicks/runs Check-Prerequisites.ps1 directly (non-elevated) on a machine that has HORIZON GRID installed already (the exact 'upgrade' scenario this script's own 'Existing installation detected' check exists to support) -- the script crashes with an unhandled UnauthorizedAccessException, emits no JSON, and returns exit code 1, which a caller would misinterpret as 'hard prerequisite failure' when no real checks even ran.
proposed_fix: Wrap the Test-Path call (and ideally the whole script body) in try/catch, treating an access-denied result the same as 'cannot determine, informational only' rather than letting it propagate.

verdict.reasoning: Empirically reproduced on this Windows machine: with $ErrorActionPreference='Stop' (set script-wide at line 34, no top-level try/catch), a Test-Path call against a path under an ACL that denies the caller's token throws a terminating error that halts all subsequent script execution (verified: code after the Test-Path call never ran). Cross-file confirmation in Common.ps1 shows Initialize-DataDirectories really does lock ProgramData\IOC Intelligence Platform (the exact $dataDir used at line 133-134 of Check-Prerequisites.ps1) to Administrators+SYSTEM only via `icacls /inheritance:r /grant:r`, and Common.ps1's own Assert-Elevated docstring explicitly warns that a UAC-filtered admin token is deny-only against that exact ACL and states 'every script that reads or writes that file needs to call this first.' Check-Prerequisites.ps1 does not dot-source Common.ps1, does not call Assert-Elevated, and has no try/catch around the Test-Path call (its only two try/catch blocks wrap unrelated docker.exe calls). The two actual current callers (installer.iss, which has PrivilegesRequired=admin, and Diagnostics.ps1, which calls Assert-Elevated before invoking this script) are unaffected, but the script's own docstring explicitly documents and invites a third, standalone 'administrator for diagnostics' invocation mode that is not protected — matching the reviewer's failure scenario exactly. This is a genuine, deterministic contract-breaking bug confined to a realistic, explicitly-documented usage path (any admin who runs the script directly without explicit 'Run as Administrator' on a machine with a prior install). It doesn't match any of the eight known intentional design patterns. P1 is appropriate: real, deterministic, contract-violating, and hits the highest-value scenario (upgrade detection), but not P0 since there's no data loss/security exposure and the two real production call paths are already safe.

title: Browser is always opened to hardcoded localhost:3000, ignoring a customized HOST_PORT_FRONTEND
actual_behavior: Lines 63 and 149 both call `Start-Process "http://localhost:3000"` with a literal, hardcoded port. `Test-FrontendHealth` (Common.ps1) also hardcodes `param([string]$BaseUrl = "http://localhost:3000")` with no lookup of the actual configured port -- unlike `Test-BackendHealth`, which correctly calls `Get-ConfiguredBackendPort` to read `HOST_PORT_BACKEND` from the .env. There is no `Get-ConfiguredFrontendPort` equivalent anywhere in the Windows scripts (confirmed by search), even though `HOST_PORT_FRONTEND` is a real, wizard-writable setting (Write-EnvFile.ps1 line 78) that docker-compose.yml actually uses (`"${HOST_PORT_FRONTEND:-3000}:3000"`), and Check-Prerequisites.ps1's own port-check explicitly documents that 'the setup wizard will offer an alternate port' on conflict.
intended_behavior: If the frontend port was remapped away from 3000 during setup (a supported, documented flow for resolving a port conflict), Open-Platform.ps1 should detect health and open the browser against the REAL configured port, matching the fix already applied for the backend port.
failure_scenario: Install-time port conflict causes the wizard to remap HOST_PORT_FRONTEND to e.g. 3001. From then on: Test-FrontendHealth always checks port 3000 (nothing listens there), so the 'waiting for healthy' loop (lines 133-138) always times out after 3 minutes and shows the 'did not report healthy' warning even though the platform is genuinely healthy on 3001; and even if it didn't time out, `Start-Process "http://localhost:3000"` would open the wrong/unreachable URL -- precisely the 'staring at a connection-refused page with zero indication of what to do' failure this script's own docstring says it exists to prevent.
proposed_fix: Add a Get-ConfiguredFrontendPort helper (mirroring Get-ConfiguredBackendPort) in Common.ps1, use it in Test-FrontendHealth's default BaseUrl, and build the Start-Process URL from the same configured port instead of a literal string.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code reading. Common.ps1 defines Get-ConfiguredBackendPort (reads HOST_PORT_BACKEND from .env) and Test-BackendHealth correctly uses it as its default BaseUrl. Test-FrontendHealth (Common.ps1 line 329) hardcodes param([string]$BaseUrl = "http://localhost:3000") with no equivalent Get-ConfiguredFrontendPort helper anywhere in the codebase (confirmed via grep across windows/scripts and windows/wizard). Open-Platform.ps1 lines 63 and 149 both call Start-Process "http://localhost:3000" as a literal string. This is not hypothetical: Setup-Wizard.ps1 (lines 1368-1384) runs a live Test-PortFree check on PortFrontend and calls Find-FreePort to remap it on conflict, exactly mirroring the backend port-conflict flow; Write-EnvFile.ps1 line 78 writes the resolved HOST_PORT_FRONTEND to .env; and docker-compose.yml line 323 ("${HOST_PORT_FRONTEND:-3000}:3000") actually publishes the container on that configured host port. So after any install that hits a frontend port conflict (a real, documented, wizard-driven flow), Test-FrontendHealth/Open-Platform.ps1 permanently check/open the wrong port. Notably, Setup-Wizard.ps1's own completion-page links (lines 1746, 1751, 1788) correctly use $State.Settings.PortFrontend, showing the omission in Open-Platform.ps1/Common.ps1/Service-Status.ps1 (which also calls Test-FrontendHealth) is a genuine miss rather than intentional design -- it doesn't match any of the listed known-intentional patterns. Impact is real but bounded: it only affects installs where the frontend port was remapped, it degrades the 'Open Platform' shortcut and health-check UX (false 'unhealthy' timeout, wrong/unreachable URL) rather than causing data loss, security exposure, or a crash, and there are user-visible fallbacks (address bar, or the wizard's own correct completion-page link). That impact profile matches the P1 the original reviewer assigned, consistent with the already-fixed backend counterpart's severity -- not P0 (no security/data-loss/crash), not lower since it fully breaks the primary convenience feature for the affected install segment.

title: Diagnostics archive is written world-readable to /tmp with no permission hardening, unlike the root-only 0700/0600 model used everywhere else in this toolchain
intended_behavior: Per common.sh's own stated model, anything holding installation/runtime state is deliberately root-only (0700 dirs, 0600 .env) precisely because /opt-style world-readable locations would leak data to any local user. The diagnostics bundle explicitly claims to be safe to share ('it contains no real credential values').
actual_behavior: `tar -czf "$ARCHIVE" ...` at line 63 creates the file under root's default umask (typically 022 -> mode 644, world-readable) at a fixed, predictable path under /tmp, and the script never chmods it afterward. The archive bundles the full last-200-lines of every container's logs (postgres, redis, neo4j, opensearch, backend, frontend, celery_worker, celery_beat) unredacted -- only the .env excerpt is actually redacted (lines 30-45); nothing sanitizes the container logs themselves.
failure_scenario: Any other local account on the host (a second sudoer, a shared support/ops login, or a compromised low-privilege service account) can run `cat /tmp/horizon-grid-diagnostics-*.tar.gz` at any point between when root runs `horizon-grid diagnostics` and whenever the file is transferred off-box/deleted, exposing internal stack traces, IOC values under active investigation, and any request/response detail application code happens to log at INFO/ERROR/DEBUG -- a materially broader exposure than the 'no real credential values' guarantee the script prints actually covers.
proposed_fix: chmod 600 "$ARCHIVE" immediately after tar succeeds (and consider placing it under $HORIZON_GRID_DATA_DIR or a root-only-created temp dir instead of the shared, world-traversable /tmp).

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading linux/scripts/diagnostics.sh in full: line 62 builds a fixed, predictable path directly under /tmp ($ARCHIVE=/tmp/horizon-grid-diagnostics-<timestamp>.tar.gz), line 63 creates it via a bare `tar -czf` with no chmod call anywhere before or after in the script (verified all 68 lines -- rm -rf on line 64 only removes the scratch OUT_DIR, never touches ARCHIVE's mode), so the archive is left at root's default umask-derived mode (typically 644) inside the world-traversable, sticky-bit-only /tmp, and persists there indefinitely since nothing in the script or its callers (grep across the repo found no wrapper that moves/chmods/deletes it afterward) ever tightens or removes it. This is a genuine inconsistency with this codebase's own explicitly-stated security model: common.sh's header comment and hg_init_data_directories/hg_sync_compose_env_file explicitly chmod 700/600 specifically because "/opt is typically 0755 root:root, i.e. world-readable, so an unprotected copy there would leak every credential to any local user" -- the exact same reasoning applies to /tmp here, but was not applied. The finding's second claim -- that only the .env excerpt (lines 30-45) is redacted while the container logs collected in lines 22-25 are not sanitized at all -- is also confirmed by reading the file; no redaction pass over logs-*.txt exists. Cross-checking windows/scripts/Diagnostics.ps1 (the script this one "mirrors") strengthens this further: the Windows side has an extensive, explicitly-tested secondary regex-redaction pass over every collected .txt file (including logs), added specifically because the developers "confirmed live" that this application's own logs can contain a raw DATABASE_URL with an embedded password and a bare API key with no label nearby. The Linux script has zero equivalent, so the risk of the world-readable /tmp archive containing literal live credentials (not just generic IOC/stack-trace telemetry) is corroborated by the project's own prior testing, not speculative. Because of that corroboration -- combined with the script's own closing message asserting "no real credential values," which could induce an admin to share the bundle even more broadly (e.g., email to external vendor support) under a false assurance -- I'm raising the severity from the original reviewer's P2 to P1: this is a realistic local-information-disclosure / credential-leak vector in a codebase that otherwise treats this exact threat model (world-readable temp/opt locations) as security-critical everywhere else, even though it still requires a second local account on the host as a precondition (keeping it short of P0).

title: Destructive restore can report success even when DROP/CREATE DATABASE silently failed or the SQL replay had mid-script errors
intended_behavior: The script's own header says it is 'Destructive by design: REPLACES the current database with whatever the backup file contains,' and the only success/failure gate it implements is RESTORE_EXIT ($? of the psql replay at line 94).
actual_behavior: Lines 90-91 (`DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS $PG_DB;` / `CREATE DATABASE $PG_DB OWNER $PG_USER;`) redirect all output to /dev/null and never check their own exit status, so if either fails (e.g. a backend connection reconnects between the pg_terminate_backend call at line 85-87 and the DROP, so DROP fails and the old database survives), the script proceeds anyway and restores into whatever database happens to exist. Separately, line 94 runs `psql -U ... -d ... <"$BACKUP_FILE"` with no `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` / `--single-transaction`. By documented psql semantics, psql only returns a non-zero exit code for a fatal error of its own or a dead connection; per-statement SQL errors during a non-interactive script are printed and then execution continues, with exit status 0 at the end. RESTORE_EXIT is checked at line 97, but RESTORE_OUTPUT's actual content is never scanned for embedded 'ERROR' lines in the success path, so it's discarded. The combined effect: a restore that drops/recreates failed (old data + new dump mixed, spurious duplicate-object errors) or a dump that fails partway through (e.g. version-mismatch or missing-extension errors on some CREATE/COPY statements) can still finish with RESTORE_EXIT=0, hitting the success branch at line 107 ('Restore complete...') and logging 'completed successfully' at line 117.
failure_scenario: Operator runs `sudo horizon-grid restore backup.sql` while a stray client (or a service that failed to stop, see related finding) reconnects to Postgres right after pg_terminate_backend runs. DROP DATABASE at line 90 fails (object in use) and is silently swallowed; CREATE DATABASE at line 91 then also fails (already exists) and is silently swallowed. The subsequent psql replay at line 94 runs against the OLD, still-populated database, throwing duplicate-key/duplicate-table errors on every CREATE/COPY that collides with pre-existing rows, but because ON_ERROR_STOP isn't set, psql exits 0 anyway. The operator sees 'Restore complete and the backend is healthy,' believing the destructive replace happened, while the database actually contains a corrupted mix of old and new data.
proposed_fix: Check the exit status of the DROP/CREATE DATABASE commands and abort with a clear error if either fails; run the restore with `psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --single-transaction` (or at minimum grep RESTORE_OUTPUT for 'ERROR' and treat that as a failure) so any mid-script SQL error is surfaced as a non-zero RESTORE_EXIT.

verdict.reasoning: Read restore-database.sh directly. Lines 90-91 (DROP/CREATE DATABASE) redirect stdout+stderr to /dev/null and never capture or check $? -- confirmed no wrapper in common.sh adds error checking to these raw `docker exec psql` calls either. Line 94's restore psql invocation has no `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` / `--single-transaction`, and per documented psql exit-code semantics (0=normal even with per-statement SQL errors printed to stderr; 3=script error only if ON_ERROR_STOP was set; 1/2 only for psql's own fatal/connection errors), RESTORE_EXIT at line 95 can be 0 despite a botched drop/recreate or a partially-failed replay. RESTORE_OUTPUT is only surfaced in the failure branch (line 100), never grepped for 'ERROR' on the success path. The race window the reviewer describes (pg_terminate_backend at 85-87 and DROP DATABASE at 90 are two separate non-atomic docker exec calls, so a stray reconnect in between can make DROP fail with Postgres's real 'database is being accessed by other users' error) is plausible, not contrived. None of the 8 documented intentional-design exceptions apply. This is a genuine error-handling gap in the sole safety gate of a script whose own header calls it 'destructive by design' -- a disaster-recovery restore can silently corrupt/mix data while still printing 'Restore complete' and logging 'completed successfully'. Severity: P1 is appropriate -- the trigger requires a specific (if realistic) race/precondition rather than being deterministic on every run (arguing against P0), but the silent-false-success consequence during a disaster-recovery operation is severe enough (no secondary signal for the operator to retry) to warrant more than P2.

title: Desktop launcher can never actually start the platform: it has no privilege-elevation mechanism, but open-platform.sh hard-requires root for the cold-start path
intended_behavior: Per the file's own header comment, this script mirrors the desktop launcher's whole job: "'click the icon' is the whole recovery story a user needs, whether that click came from a desktop menu entry or `horizon-grid open` in a terminal." `linux/horizon-grid.desktop` has `Exec=horizon-grid open` and `Terminal=false`, and `linux/bin/horizon-grid` execs this very script unmodified for the `open` subcommand -- i.e. the desktop icon's entire job is to run this file with no wrapper.
actual_behavior: When the platform is not already healthy (the exact case the desktop icon exists to fix -- machine just booted, containers stopped), line 25's fast-path check fails and execution reaches `hg_assert_root` at line 30, which (per common.sh) does `if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then echo "...Re-run with sudo." >&2; exit 1; fi`. Neither `horizon-grid.desktop`'s Exec line nor `bin/horizon-grid`'s dispatch (`exec "$SCRIPTS_DIR/open-platform.sh"`, no sudo/pkexec anywhere) elevates privileges. With Terminal=false, the stderr message is never shown to the user.
failure_scenario: User logs into their desktop after a reboot (containers stopped) and double-clicks the 'HORIZON GRID' icon. `horizon-grid open` runs as the logged-in non-root user, `hg_test_backend_health`/`hg_test_frontend_health` correctly report unhealthy, `hg_assert_root` prints its message to a stderr nobody sees and exits 1. No browser opens, no root/password prompt appears, no visible error -- the icon appears to simply do nothing, and the platform never starts. This breaks the primary, documented use case for the desktop launcher (starting a stopped platform), not just an edge case.
proposed_fix: Either wrap the desktop entry's Exec in `pkexec` (with a policy allowing it to run the compose stack), or have open-platform.sh itself invoke `pkexec`/a graphical sudo front-end when it detects it needs root and has a display, or write a small GUI notification when hg_assert_root's condition is hit under a non-interactive/no-TTY invocation.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the full chain. linux/horizon-grid.desktop has Exec=horizon-grid open, Terminal=false, and build-deb.sh installs it verbatim to /usr/share/applications/horizon-grid.desktop. linux/bin/horizon-grid's `open` case does `exec "$SCRIPTS_DIR/open-platform.sh"` with no sudo/pkexec wrapper or arguments. open-platform.sh's fast path (line 25) only skips ahead if the stack is already healthy; on the very case the launcher exists for (stopped containers after boot), execution falls through to line 30's `hg_assert_root`, which (common.sh lines 58-66) does nothing but `if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then echo ...>&2; exit 1; fi` — a plain non-root check with no elevation mechanism whatsoever. I verified there is no polkit policy file, no setuid bit set anywhere (postinst only chmods 0755, not setuid), and no sudoers entry in debian/postinst, debian/control, or build-deb.sh — grepping the entire linux/ tree turned up no polkit/pkexec/postinst-setuid logic at all. With Terminal=false the stderr message is invisible to a user who double-clicks the desktop icon, so the icon silently does nothing when the platform is stopped, which is precisely the primary use case the file's own header comment says it exists to serve ("click the icon is the whole recovery story a user needs"). This is a genuine, high-confidence bug, not one of the documented intentional design patterns. On severity: this breaks the core documented desktop-launcher use case (starting a stopped platform via double-click) with a completely silent failure (no visible error, no prompt) — a materially broken primary user-facing entry point, which is legitimately P1 (severe but has a workaround: the user can still run `sudo horizon-grid open` or `sudo horizon-grid start` from a terminal, and the platform isn't data-losing or insecure, so it doesn't rise to P0). I concur with the original reviewer's P1 rating.

title: The non-root 'already healthy' fast path silently checks the wrong port on any install with a customized frontend/backend port, so it never actually detects a running, healthy platform
intended_behavior: Lines 23-24's comment states the fast path exists so the common case (platform already running) 'shouldn't pay for a sudo prompt or a wait it doesn't need' -- i.e. hg_test_backend_health/hg_test_frontend_health should correctly detect the real running instance using the real configured HOST_PORT_FRONTEND/HOST_PORT_BACKEND from $HORIZON_GRID_ENV_FILE, exactly like every other caller of those helpers does.
actual_behavior: hg_test_backend_health/hg_test_frontend_health (common.sh) call hg_read_env_var, which does `[ -f "$HORIZON_GRID_ENV_FILE" ] || return 0` before reading. $HORIZON_GRID_ENV_FILE lives inside $HORIZON_GRID_CONFIG_DIR (/etc/horizon-grid), which both common.sh's hg_init_data_directories and setup_wizard.py (`os.chmod(d, 0o700)` for CONFIG_DIR, confirmed at setup_wizard.py line 1080) lock to `chmod 700 root:root`. A non-root process cannot even traverse into that directory, so `[ -f ... ]` fails (permission denied on path traversal) and hg_read_env_var silently returns empty -- for a non-root invocation, port always falls back to the hardcoded defaults 3000/8000 (line 12 here, and the equivalent default in common.sh's two health-check functions), never the real configured HOST_PORT_FRONTEND/HOST_PORT_BACKEND. open-platform.sh is the only caller of these two health-check functions that runs them before hg_assert_root (every other caller -- watchdog.sh, service-status.sh, service-start.sh, service-restart.sh -- calls hg_assert_root first and so always runs as root, unaffected).
failure_scenario: Setup wizard's own port-conflict resolution (hg_find_free_port / the wizard's Ports page) assigns HOST_PORT_FRONTEND=3001 because 3000 was already taken by something else on the machine, and the platform is fully up and healthy on port 3001. User double-clicks the desktop icon (runs as the non-root desktop user). Line 12's FRONTEND_PORT read returns empty (permission denied on /etc/horizon-grid), defaults to 3000; line 25's health checks probe localhost:3000/localhost:8000, which are not the real ports, get connection-refused, and report 'unhealthy' even though the platform is actually running fine on 3001. Execution falls through to hg_assert_root (line 30) and hits the P1 finding above -- so on any non-default-port install, EVERY desktop-icon click fails, not just the cold-start case.
proposed_fix: Either have open-platform.sh assert root unconditionally before doing anything (losing the no-sudo-prompt optimization but staying correct), or make the fast-path port lookup work without needing to read the root-only .env (e.g. probe both the default and a world-readable last-known-port cache written at configure time, or grant the fast-path health probe an allowed helper that runs with elevated read access only for that lookup).

verdict.reasoning:
Verified end-to-end against the actual source.

1. linux/scripts/open-platform.sh lines 12 and 25: FRONTEND_PORT is read via `hg_read_env_var HOST_PORT_FRONTEND` (defaulting to 3000 on empty), and the fast-path health check at line 25 calls `hg_test_backend_health`/`hg_test_frontend_health` with no base_url argument, so those functions do their own `hg_read_env_var` lookups (defaulting to 8000/3000) — all of this runs BEFORE `hg_assert_root` at line 30.

2. common.sh's `hg_read_env_var` (line 337-345): `[ -f "$HORIZON_GRID_ENV_FILE" ] || return 0` — silently returns empty if the file can't be stat'd, with no distinction between "file doesn't exist" and "permission denied."

3. `$HORIZON_GRID_ENV_FILE` = `$HORIZON_GRID_CONFIG_DIR/.env` = `/etc/horizon-grid/.env`. `hg_init_data_directories` (common.sh line 69-81) does `chown root:root` + `chmod 700` on `$HORIZON_GRID_CONFIG_DIR`. I independently confirmed the same lockdown in `linux/wizard/setup_wizard.py` line 1079-1080 (`os.chmod(d, 0o700)` for CONFIG_DIR, run only after `require_root()`), and again in `linux/debian/postinst` line 23 (`chmod 700 "$d"`). No group/ACL-based carve-out exists anywhere in the linux/ tree (checked for setfacl/groupadd/usermod — none). A 700 root:root directory blocks even path traversal for any non-root, non-group process, so `stat()` on the .env path fails with EACCES for a non-root caller, and bash's `[ -f ]` just reports that as false — not an error, but wrong information silently swallowed.

4. Confirmed `open-platform.sh` runs unelevated in the exact scenario the finding describes: `linux/bin/horizon-grid`'s `open)` case does a plain `exec "$SCRIPTS_DIR/open-platform.sh"` (no sudo/pkexec), and `linux/horizon-grid.desktop` has `Exec=horizon-grid open` with `Terminal=false` — i.e., the desktop-icon click path runs as the unprivileged desktop user with no elevation and no visible terminal for any stderr message.

5. Cross-checked common.sh's own comment (lines 252-260) confirming HOST_PORT_BACKEND/HOST_PORT_FRONTEND are genuinely customizable by the wizard's port-conflict resolution (`hg_find_free_port`), so this isn't a hypothetical config.

Net effect matches the finding exactly: on any install where the wizard assigned non-default ports (a realistic case, since 3000/8000 are extremely common dev-tool ports likely to already be taken on a workstation), a non-root double-click of the desktop icon (or a plain terminal `horizon-grid open`) will always probe the wrong (default) ports, always see the real, healthy service as "down," fall through to `hg_assert_root` at line 30, and exit 1 with no browser opened — silently, since `Terminal=false` swallows the stderr message for the GUI path. Re-running via `sudo horizon-grid open` does work (root can read the real env file), so there is a workaround, just a non-obvious one for the primary desktop-icon flow this script exists to serve.

Severity: I'm keeping the original P1 rating. It's not P0 — no security/data-loss impact, and a workaround exists (sudo via terminal). But it's a genuine, deterministic (not edge-case-rare) break of the single primary "click icon to open the app" user flow for any customized-port install, with zero visible feedback in the GUI-launch case, which is squarely a high/P1-level functional defect rather than P2/cosmetic.

title: No signal trap / atomic-write pattern: an interrupted backup leaves a partial, unhardened dump file that later gets picked up as 'the most recent backup'
intended_behavior: Every backup file that survives in $HORIZON_GRID_BACKUPS_DIR should be a complete, valid pg_dump snapshot, since restore-database.sh's no-argument invocation blindly picks `ls -1t .../postgres-*.sql | head -n1` (restore-database.sh line 35) as 'the most recent backup' without any integrity check.
actual_behavior: The script sets `set -u` only (no `trap`, no `set -e`) and writes directly to the final path `$DUMP_PATH` via shell redirection at line 49 (`>"$DUMP_PATH"`), with `chmod 600` only applied after a full successful run (line 50) and cleanup (`rm -f "$DUMP_PATH"`) only reached in the explicit non-zero-exit/empty-file `else` branch (lines 57-61). If the script (or the `docker exec` it runs) is interrupted by SIGINT/SIGTERM or the process is killed mid-dump, execution never reaches either the success block or the else block, so a truncated dump file is left on disk at its final filename, with default (not 600) permissions, and is never pruned or flagged as bad.
failure_scenario: An operator (or the packaging's own upgrade flow, which per common.sh's header comment calls this before an upgrade) Ctrl+C's or the process is killed (e.g. OOM, systemd unit timeout) while `docker exec ... pg_dump ...` is mid-stream. `postgres-20260904-120000.sql` is left behind, truncated, at default permissions. Later, `sudo horizon-grid restore` with no arguments picks exactly this truncated file as the newest backup and feeds it into psql (which, per the related restore-database.sh finding, does not use ON_ERROR_STOP), so the restore appears to 'complete' while actually only partially replaying the truncated dump.
proposed_fix: Write to a temp path (e.g. `$DUMP_PATH.tmp`) and `mv` into place only after `[ -s ... ]` succeeds; add a `trap 'rm -f "$DUMP_PATH" "$DUMP_PATH.tmp"' INT TERM` (or EXIT, guarded by a completion flag) so an interrupted run can't leave a plausible-looking-but-broken file behind.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of both scripts plus common.sh.

backup-database.sh (full file read): line 8 sets `set -u` only — no `trap` anywhere in the file, no `set -e`. Line 49 pipes `docker exec ... pg_dump` output directly into the FINAL filename via `>"$DUMP_PATH"` (no temp file). `chmod 600` (line 50) and the pruning of old backups (line 56) only run inside the success branch of the `if`. `rm -f "$DUMP_PATH"` (line 60) only runs in the explicit `else` branch, reached only when `pg_dump` exits with a real nonzero code or leaves an empty file — never reached if the script itself is killed by a signal (SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGKILL) mid-dump, since without a trap, bash's default action for those signals terminates the script immediately rather than falling through to any cleanup code. common.sh (full file read) confirms no global trap is set anywhere either (its own comment even explains `set -u` is deliberately not global, with no mention of a trap).

restore-database.sh (full file read) confirms the exact claimed consumption path: line 35, `ls -1t "$HORIZON_GRID_BACKUPS_DIR"/postgres-*.sql | head -n1`, picks purely by mtime with zero integrity check (only an existence check, `[ -f "$BACKUP_FILE" ]`, at line 43). Critically, I found the impact is actually worse than the finding describes: restore-database.sh unconditionally DROPs and recreates the target database (lines 90-91) *before* attempting to stream the backup file into `psql` (line 94). So even setting aside the separate ON_ERROR_STOP issue, feeding a truncated/partial dump into this flow destroys the prior database first — any operator who lets a truncated "most recent" backup get picked has already lost data the moment the restore begins, independent of whether psql later reports an error.

I also found a concrete, realistic trigger that the original reviewer only gestured at generically: `linux/systemd/horizon-grid-backup.service` runs the unattended nightly backup as `Type=oneshot` with `TimeoutStartSec=120` — any `pg_dump` run that exceeds 120 seconds (plausible as the platform's case/investigation data grows over time) gets systemd-terminated mid-dump, with no corresponding `hg_log` ERROR line ever written (that only fires from the unreachable `else` branch), so the failure is completely silent from the application's own log's perspective. `setup_wizard.py`'s `_backup_before_upgrade()` (confirmed via read, lines 803-828) also invokes this script synchronously before every upgrade, a second real-world call site. I confirmed via grep that no other file in `linux/` performs any checksum/size/integrity validation on these dump files anywhere in the pipeline.

Severity: the original P2 undersells this. The trigger is not just an unlikely manual Ctrl-C — it's baked into the only unattended backup mechanism via a hardcoded 120s timeout that will eventually be exceeded on any successfully-growing production install, the failure is silent (no error log entry at all, unlike the explicit-failure path), and because restore drops the database before restoring, using the resulting corrupt "most recent" backup causes irreversible data loss in exactly the disaster-recovery scenario backups exist to protect against. I'm upgrading this to P1.

title: Prod override's backend command drops msfrpcd startup, breaking Metasploit exploit validation on every real install
intended_behavior: The backend container should start msfrpcd (bound to 127.0.0.1:55553, the transport backend/app/pentest/msf_client.py talks to for the admin-gated, real Metasploit exploit-validation feature) in the background, then run migrations, then start uvicorn -- exactly what docker-compose.yml's own backend `command:` (lines 242-245) does: `sh -c "msfrpcd -f -P \"$$MSF_RPC_PASSWORD\" -S -a 127.0.0.1 -p 55553 -U msf & alembic upgrade head && uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload"`.
actual_behavior: docker-compose.prod.yml overrides `backend.command` with `sh -c "alembic upgrade head && uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000"` -- it drops the `msfrpcd -f -P ... &` prefix entirely. Docker Compose merges `command:` as a scalar override (full replacement, not append/merge), so under the exact invocation this file's own header documents (`docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d --build`), and which windows/scripts/Common.ps1 (line 205) and linux/scripts/common.sh both actually run for every real install, msfrpcd is never started inside the backend container.
failure_scenario: An administrator installs Horizon Grid via the Windows or Linux installer (both invoke docker compose with this exact -f/-f combination), then opens the Pentest Suite and tries to run the admin-gated real Metasploit exploit-validation feature on a finding. backend/app/pentest/msf_client.py's MsfRpcClient tries to reach 127.0.0.1:55553 inside the backend container, gets connection-refused (nothing listens there), and raises MsfRpcError('msfrpcd unreachable: ...'); is_available() swallows that and reports Metasploit as unavailable with no msfrpcd-specific diagnostic. The entire real-exploit-execution capability that v0.3.0 shipped is silently non-functional in every real production/installer deployment, while it works fine when a developer runs plain `docker compose up` (docker-compose.yml alone) against the dev tree -- so this regression would not be caught by testing that only exercises the dev compose file directly.
proposed_fix: Keep the msfrpcd prefix in the prod override, e.g.: `command: > sh -c "msfrpcd -f -P \"$$MSF_RPC_PASSWORD\" -S -a 127.0.0.1 -p 55553 -U msf & alembic upgrade head && uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000"` (identical to the base file's command minus `--reload`).

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading. docker-compose.prod.yml lines 25-27 set backend.command to `sh -c "alembic upgrade head && uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000"`, a full scalar replacement of docker-compose.yml's own backend command (lines 242-245: `sh -c "msfrpcd -f -P ... -a 127.0.0.1 -p 55553 -U msf & alembic upgrade head && uvicorn ... --reload"`). Docker Compose merges `command:` as a full override, not an append, so the msfrpcd startup is entirely dropped under the prod override. Verified the base Dockerfile's own CMD (`CMD ["uvicorn", ...]`) has no msfrpcd fallback either -- docker-compose.yml's command: field is the only place msfrpcd is ever started, so there is no other mechanism that would launch it. Verified both installer scripts invoke exactly `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml ... up -d` (windows/scripts/Common.ps1 and linux/scripts/common.sh line 215), i.e. every real production/installer deployment applies this override. Verified backend/app/pentest/msf_client.py's get_client() defaults (backend/app/core/config.py: msf_rpc_host=127.0.0.1, msf_rpc_port=55553) target exactly the address msfrpcd would have bound to, and MsfRpcClient._raw_call wraps httpx connection failures in MsfRpcError('msfrpcd unreachable: ...'), while is_available() catches all exceptions and silently returns False. So under any real install, the admin-gated Metasploit exploit-validation feature will report 'unavailable' with no specific diagnostic, while a plain dev `docker compose up` (base file only) works fine -- exactly the asymmetry claimed. This isn't covered by any of the listed intentional-design exceptions. Severity: P1 is appropriate -- it silently and completely breaks one specific, real, already-shipped feature (Metasploit exploit validation) in every production install, but it's a single gated feature behind graceful degradation (not a security hole, crash, or data-loss issue, and not the whole app), so P0 would overstate it while P1 correctly reflects a significant broken capability in every real deployment.

title: Readiness/liveness probes hit the dependency-free /health, not /health/detailed
intended_behavior: backend/app/main.py explicitly documents that 'Windows/Linux watchdog scripts and the Docker Compose healthcheck: block should point [at /health/detailed], not at the plain /health' because /health 'unconditionally returned {"status": "ok"} regardless of any real dependency, confirmed live to still return 200 with Postgres fully stopped'. The docker-compose backend healthcheck this file is translated from does in fact target http://localhost:8000/health/detailed for exactly that reason (its own comment: 'Hits /health/detailed (real Postgres/Redis check), not plain /health').
actual_behavior: Both readinessProbe (lines 43-50) and livenessProbe (lines 51-58) call httpGet path /health, the shallow liveness-only endpoint that never checks Postgres or Redis.
failure_scenario: Postgres becomes unreachable after the backend pod has already passed its first probe (crash, PVC full, credentials rotated wrong, network policy change, etc). /health keeps returning 200 unconditionally, so the readinessProbe never removes the pod from the backend Service's endpoints and the livenessProbe never restarts it, even though main.py's own comment states Postgres is 'load-bearing for virtually every endpoint'. Every DB-backed request served by that pod now 500s while Kubernetes considers the pod perfectly healthy, and no self-healing action is ever triggered.
proposed_fix: Point both probes at /health/detailed (and treat its 503 as failing readiness; consider keeping liveness on /health if you want to avoid a Postgres outage causing a pointless restart storm).

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the actual files. k8s/base/backend-deployment.yaml lines 43-58 have both readinessProbe and livenessProbe hitting path: /health. backend/app/main.py's /health handler (line 410) is explicitly documented as 'Deliberately dependency-free' with no Postgres/Redis check, while /health/detailed (line 430) actually pings Postgres and Redis and returns 503 if Postgres is down -- and its docstring explicitly states 'Windows/Linux watchdog scripts and the Docker Compose healthcheck: block should point here, not at the plain /health above.' docker-compose.yml line 232 confirms the compose healthcheck does target /health/detailed for this exact reason. The k8s deployment file's own header comment frames itself as a 'Translation of docker-compose backend service,' yet the probes silently diverge from the compose healthcheck's target with no comment justifying it as intentional -- this doesn't match any of the eight documented intentional design patterns. This is a real regression: with a shared Postgres dependency across 2 replicas, a Postgres outage (or a per-pod network/credential issue) after pods are already Ready will never cause k8s to mark the pod NotReady or restart it, because /health always returns 200 regardless of DB state, defeating the readiness-based traffic-shifting mechanism the app's own comments describe as necessary. One nuance: the reviewer's proposed fix bundles livenessProbe together with readinessProbe, but per k8s best practice, liveness generally should NOT depend on external services (to avoid restart storms) -- the reviewer themselves hedges this in the proposed fix text. The core, unambiguous defect is the readinessProbe pointing at the shallow endpoint, which is a genuine, documented-against regression with real multi-replica traffic-routing impact, supporting the P1 rating as claimed.

title: No client-side way to supply ioc_type_hint, so any dot-free IOC value (threat actor, malware family, campaign, mutex, service name) permanently 422s
actual_behavior: StreamLookupOptions/streamLookup() only ever sends {value, provider_ids, ai_backend} to POST /lookup/stream (frontend/lib/api.ts:205-231); ioc_type_hint is never included anywhere in the frontend (confirmed via repo-wide search -- the only two frontend hits for 'ioc_type_hint' are comments, not a parameter). backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py:85-87 does `ioc_type = payload.ioc_type_hint or detect_ioc_type(ioc_value)` and raises HTTPException(422, 'Could not determine IOC type; pass ioc_type_hint.') when detection fails. backend/app/ioc/detector.py:150-158 explicitly returns IOCType.UNKNOWN for any single-token, dot-free string (its own comment: 'could be malware family, threat actor, campaign name, process name, mutex, or service name... default to UNKNOWN and let the user's provider selection / context disambiguate') -- but no such disambiguation UI or parameter exists anywhere in the frontend.
failure_scenario: An analyst types a threat-actor name like 'APT28' or 'Lazarus' into the search bar (frontend/components/dashboard/TopSearchBar.tsx, whose own placeholder text explicitly invites 'IP, domain, URL, hash, CVE, threat actor, YARA rule...'). The request 422s with 'Could not determine IOC type; pass ioc_type_hint.' frontend/lib/api.ts:260 correctly surfaces that detail message via onError, but there is no UI control, dialog, or type-selector anywhere that lets the analyst actually supply ioc_type_hint -- the investigation can never be started for this entire class of IOC, despite the feature being advertised in the search placeholder and IOCType.THREAT_ACTOR/MALWARE_FAMILY/CAMPAIGN being real, first-class node types elsewhere in the correlation graph and evidence model.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the actual code. frontend/lib/api.ts:205-231 (StreamLookupOptions/streamLookup) only ever accepts providerIds and aiBackend and only ever sends {value, provider_ids, ai_backend} in the POST /lookup/stream body -- ioc_type_hint is never a field on the request. A repo-wide grep for ioc_type_hint/iocTypeHint/typeHint across frontend/ turns up zero real usages (only comments/docs, and one unrelated match in RelationshipGraph.tsx that's just a comment about IOCType visual-family grouping for graph nodes). The actual call site (frontend/app/lookup/new/page.tsx:103-140) invokes streamLookup(rawValue.trim(), handlers, controller.signal) with no options argument at all, and TopSearchBar.tsx's placeholder text explicitly invites 'IP, domain, URL, hash, CVE, threat actor, YARA rule...' with no accompanying type-selector UI anywhere nearby. I also checked basket/page.tsx (the other endpoint, BasketAddRequest, that accepts ioc_type_hint) and it likewise has no hint-supplying control -- it only displays an already-computed threat_actors field, not an input. On the backend, backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py:85-87 does exactly `ioc_type = payload.ioc_type_hint or detect_ioc_type(ioc_value)` followed by `raise HTTPException(422, ...)` on failure, and backend/app/ioc/detector.py's single-token/dot-free branch (matching `^[\w\-\.]+$` with no dot) explicitly returns IOCType.UNKNOWN unless the string ends in .exe/.dll/.sys -- so a value like 'APT28' or 'Lazarus' hits UNKNOWN and 422s every time, with no client-side way to supply the hint that would fix it. This is a real, reproducible, permanent dead end for an entire advertised IOC class (threat actor, malware family, campaign, mutex, service name), with no UI workaround -- it does not match any of the eight listed intentional-design patterns. Severity: P1 is appropriate as claimed. It is not P0 (no security breach, data loss, or full outage -- other IOC types work fine and the API itself supports the hint), but it silently breaks a whole class of the product's own core, explicitly-advertised functionality (threat-intel correlation for actors/malware/campaigns) with zero UI workaround, surfaced only as a confusing generic 422 detail message.

title: AI provider list has no merge-with-registry fallback, unlike the IOC provider list -- new AI backends become permanently unreachable via the UI on any upgraded install
actual_behavior: list_ai_providers() (runtime_config.py:218-223) just SELECTs whatever rows already exist in provider_runtime_configs for kind=AI and returns them -- nothing merges in the full app/core/runtime_config.py:29 AI_BACKENDS list for backends that have no row yet. Its route (backend/app/api/routes/runtime.py:26-28, GET /runtime/ai-providers) returns that result verbatim. Contrast with the IOC provider route (routes/runtime.py:101-130, GET /runtime/ioc-providers), which explicitly merges `known = {p.provider_id: p for p in get_all_providers()}` with the DB rows so every registered IOC provider shows up even with zero configuration. Rows are only ever created for ALL 11 AI backends at once by seed_from_env_if_empty() (runtime_config.py:501-547), which app/main.py:298-308 documents as "a no-op on every subsequent restart once the table has any row at all" -- there is no per-backend backfill when AI_BACKENDS grows. The frontend never works around this either: AiQuickSwitch.tsx's dropdown (`providers.map(...)`) and providers/page.tsx's AI Providers tab (`aiProviders.map(...)`) both iterate ONLY over whatever listAIProviders() returned; there is no client-side merge against a static list of all 11 backend ids, and there is no "Add Provider" affordance anywhere in the frontend that would let an operator create a first row for a backend not already present.
failure_scenario: This codebase's own comments (connection_test.py's module docstring: "none of the original five AI backends... had ANY live connection test before this file existed... now six, with OpenAI added"; kimi/deepseek/xai/mistral/openrouter clients all added later still) show AI_BACKENDS grew over time from 5 to 11. Any real deployment that was already running (and had therefore already populated provider_runtime_configs) before kimi/deepseek/xai/mistral/openrouter (and initially openai) were added to AI_BACKENDS will never get DB rows for those backends created by seeding. On that install, AiQuickSwitch's dropdown and the /providers Manage Providers AI tab permanently show only the originally-seeded backends -- Kimi/DeepSeek/Grok/Mistral/OpenRouter/OpenAI are completely invisible and unconfigurable through any UI path, even though the backend route (POST /runtime/ai-providers/{backend}) and every *_client.py module fully support them.

verdict.reasoning:
Read backend/app/core/runtime_config.py, backend/app/api/routes/runtime.py, backend/app/main.py, and the two frontend files cited. Every factual claim in the finding checks out against the actual code:

1. runtime_config.py:218-223 `list_ai_providers()` is a bare `SELECT ... WHERE kind == ProviderKind.AI` with no merge against the `AI_BACKENDS` list (line 29). It returns exactly whatever rows exist.
2. routes/runtime.py:26-28 `GET /runtime/ai-providers` returns `await svc.list_ai_providers()` verbatim -- no merge happens at the route layer either.
3. Contrast confirmed: routes/runtime.py:101-130 `list_ioc_providers` explicitly builds `known = {p.provider_id: p for p in get_all_providers()}` and synthesizes a placeholder entry for any provider with no DB row, guaranteeing every registered IOC provider is visible regardless of DB state. No equivalent exists for AI.
4. `seed_from_env_if_empty()` (runtime_config.py:501-551) only acts `if existing is not None: return False` -- i.e., it is a strict one-shot seed for a completely empty table, never a per-backend backfill. main.py:298-308's docstring independently confirms this is "a no-op on every subsequent restart once the table has any row at all."
5. The historical growth claim is independently corroborated by app/ai/connection_test.py's own docstring: "none of the original five AI backends... (now six, with OpenAI added)" -- confirming AI_BACKENDS grew over time (now 11 per line 29, with kimi/deepseek/xai/mistral/openrouter/openai added later).
6. Frontend confirmed: AiQuickSwitch.tsx's dropdown (`providers.map(...)`) and providers/page.tsx's AI tab (`aiProviders.map(...)`) both iterate purely over whatever `listAIProviders()` returns, with no static fallback list and no "Add Provider" control for AI (unlike IOC, which doesn't need one because the backend already synthesizes the full list).

Net effect: on any install whose provider_runtime_configs table was already populated (by the one-time seed) before newer entries were added to AI_BACKENDS/_AI_ENV_SEED_MAP, those newer backends get no DB row, ever, and are therefore invisible in every UI surface that lists AI providers. This is a genuine schema/behavior asymmetry between the AI and IOC list paths, not one of the documented intentional patterns (it doesn't match any of items 1-8 in the known-patterns list). The backend POST route itself does support any backend in AI_BACKENDS, so a raw API call is a viable admin workaround, which keeps this from being a P0 (no data loss, no security impact, no total outage) -- but there is no discoverable UI path to reach it, which matches a P1 (major functionality gap on a real, plausible upgrade path for this project, given its documented dual-source-tree deploy model of propagating new backend code into an already-seeded installed copy).

title: CIDR-typed targets never go through the RFC1918/global-routability check every other scannable type gets
actual_behavior: In _validate_scope(), the IOCType.CIDR branch (lines 260-275) only parses the network and enforces the /28 address cap; it never calls assert_globally_routable_target. Only the elif branch for IPV4/IPV6/DOMAIN/HOSTNAME/URL (line 276 onward) calls assert_globally_routable_target/assert_valid_hostname_syntax to reject RFC1918/loopback-adjacent/link-local/reserved destinations. nmap_tool.py (the only tool that supports IOCType.CIDR) takes the CIDR string verbatim as its nmap argv target, so whatever range passed the size cap gets scanned with no destination check at all.
failure_scenario: An analyst (no admin rights needed) calls POST /api/v1/lookup/stream with ioc_type_hint="cidr" and value e.g. "172.19.0.0/28" (this platform's own docker-compose bridge range) or any other internal /28, then POST /api/v1/security-assessment/{lookup_id}/run with tool_ids=["nmap"]. _validate_scope accepts it (network parses, <=16 addresses), and nmap actually port-scans the internal Docker network -- exactly the class of SSRF assert_globally_routable_target's own docstring says it exists to prevent (the 'opensearch:9200' incident), just reached via CIDR instead of a single host/domain/URL. The project's own unit tests prove this is not merely theoretical: test_rejects_private_rfc1918_ipv4_target (test_security_assessment_service.py) rejects a plain IPv4 172.19.0.5 as private, while test_accepts_a_small_cidr_at_exactly_the_cap in the same file explicitly accepts CIDR 10.0.0.0/28 (an equally RFC1918 range) with zero destination check -- and the surrounding comment even states this function 'only ever format/destination-validat[es] the CIDR IOC type' for the size cap, not the destination.
proposed_fix: In the CIDR branch, resolve/iterate the network's member addresses (or at least check the network's own prefix) through the same is_global-based check assert_globally_routable_target already implements for the other types, rejecting a CIDR that is not entirely globally-routable (with the same explicit loopback carve-out already used elsewhere).

verdict.reasoning: Read security_assessment.py lines 250-304 directly: the CIDR branch (260-275) only performs ipaddress.ip_network parsing and the /28 size-cap check; it never calls assert_globally_routable_target/assert_valid_hostname_syntax, which are only invoked in the elif branch for IPV4/IPV6/DOMAIN/HOSTNAME/URL (276-304). The inline comment claims url_safety.py's docstrings justify exempting CIDR, but reading url_safety.py in full shows its docstrings only justify exempting the separate Pentest Suite (which has its own scope-based authorization model) -- there is no stated rationale for exempting CIDR within the same Security Assessment Toolkit, and assert_globally_routable_target's own docstring states the toolkit's targets should never resolve to non-global infrastructure, a rationale that applies equally to CIDR. Confirmed in nmap_tool.py that CIDR is a supported_type and the raw CIDR string is passed verbatim as the final argv element to the real nmap subprocess, with the only validation being a leading-'-' injection check -- no RFC1918/loopback/link-local guard. Confirmed via the existing test file that test_rejects_private_rfc1918_ipv4_target rejects plain IPv4 172.19.0.5 while test_accepts_a_small_cidr_at_exactly_the_cap accepts the equally-private 10.0.0.0/28 CIDR with zero destination check, exactly the asymmetry the finding describes. This does not match any of the listed known-intentional design patterns; pattern (5) explicitly carves out reporting a shared-tool bug when one feature's specific use is broken, which is the case here (nmap within the Security Assessment Toolkit, not the Pentest Suite). This is a real, demonstrable SSRF-class internal-network-scanning gap reachable by any non-admin analyst with security_assessment:create permission. Severity: bounded impact (nmap's hardcoded profiles exclude -O/-sS/-sU/--script/OS-fingerprinting, so only port/service enumeration across up to 16 internal addresses is possible, not RCE) but a genuine, meaningful internal reconnaissance/lateral-movement enabler matching the class of issue the codebase's own docstrings say assert_globally_routable_target exists to prevent -- P1 as claimed is an appropriate severity, not P0 (no RCE) and not P2 (real, exploitable, non-admin-reachable network boundary bypass).

title: Finalization block (persist findings + flip to COMPLETED) in _execute_run has no exception/cancellation guard, unlike the tool-execution phase above it
actual_behavior: The try/except at lines 397-452 only wraps the tool-execution loop and explicitly handles both asyncio.CancelledError and Exception, writing a terminal CANCELLED/FAILED status either way. The subsequent block (lines 454-506) that adds SecurityAssessmentFinding/ProviderResultRecord rows and flips the run's status to COMPLETED is a bare `async with new_session() as db: ... await db.commit()` with no try/except of any kind. If a cancellation lands in this window (cancel_run()'s task.cancel() can be delivered at any await point, including here), or if any ordinary exception occurs (DB error, connection blip) during this specific block, the exception propagates straight out of _execute_run uncaught. The row is still status=RUNNING at that point, and nothing else in the process will ever write to it again.
failure_scenario: A user clicks 'Cancel Scan' at the exact moment a run's tools have all finished and _execute_run is in the middle of persisting findings/updating status (a real, non-instantaneous window: multiple db.add() calls plus an awaited db.execute/db.commit round-trip). The CancelledError propagates uncaught; the freshly-computed findings are rolled back (never committed); the run's row is left at status=RUNNING forever with a live 'Cancel Scan' button that will keep hitting cancel_run()'s 'not tracked' branch (since the task has already finished and been discarded from _run_tasks) -- clicking Cancel again happens to self-heal it via the guarded direct-DB-write path, but nothing in the UI or backend ever tells the user to do that, and the real scan findings are permanently lost. Absent a second manual cancel click, the row is genuinely stuck until the next full backend restart's orphan-recovery sweep in main.py, which then mislabels it 'Orphaned by an unclean shutdown' even though the process never crashed.
proposed_fix: Wrap the findings-persistence + status-finalization block in the same try/except CancelledError / except Exception pattern already used for the tool-execution phase, so any failure there also writes a guarded terminal FAILED/CANCELLED status instead of leaving the row RUNNING.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading of security_assessment.py lines 379-529: the only try/except in _execute_run spans lines 397-452 (tool-execution loop only, with explicit CancelledError and Exception handlers that both terminate the function after writing a guarded terminal status). The finalization block at 454-506 (persisting SecurityAssessmentFinding/ProviderResultRecord rows and flipping status to COMPLETED via a guarded update+commit) sits outside that try, at the same indentation level, with no exception handling of its own (the only other try/except in the function, at 525-527, wraps solely the post-completion _refresh_lookup_assessment call, not the finalization block). Verified via app/core/db.py that new_session() returns a plain AsyncSession whose context-manager exit-on-exception closes (and thus rolls back) uncommitted adds, confirming that a CancelledError or DB error landing on any await in this block (session open, db.execute at 494, db.commit at 500) discards the just-computed findings and propagates uncaught out of _execute_run. Verified via _spawn_background's done_callback (lines 77-88) that the task is deregistered from _run_tasks the instant it finishes this way, so a later cancel_run() call takes the untracked-task branch and self-heals the row via its own guarded direct DB write — matching the reviewer's exact described behavior.
