title: http_headers_tool follows redirects with no re-validation of each hop against the SSRF scope check
actual_behavior: httpx.AsyncClient is constructed with follow_redirects=True (lines 48 and 53) and no event_hooks/max_redirects restriction anywhere in the codebase (confirmed via search) validate the destination of each redirect hop. Only the ORIGINAL target string is checked by assert_globally_routable_target in core/security_assessment.py, before this tool ever runs.
failure_scenario: The Security Assessment Toolkit's whole purpose is investigating potentially-malicious external domains/IPs -- targets whose operators are adversarial by definition. A malicious target passes the upstream globally-routable check (its own server has a real public IP), but when the tool sends its one GET request, that server responds with a 30x redirect to an internal address (e.g. a docker-compose service name reachable from the backend container, or a cloud metadata endpoint such as 169.254.169.254 if deployed in a cloud VM). httpx transparently follows it and the tool reports the internal response's headers/status back to the analyst as if they belonged to the original target -- the exact SSRF class url_safety.py's own docstring says it fixed for the direct-target case (the 'opensearch:9200' incident), reopened here via a redirect instead of the initial hostname.
proposed_fix: Either disable follow_redirects and report the redirect itself as a finding, or use an httpx event_hook / manual redirect loop that re-runs assert_globally_routable_target against each Location header's resolved host before following it.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading the actual files.

http_headers_tool.py (lines 41-63) builds `url` from the raw `target` string and, on both the primary path (line 48) and the http:// fallback path (line 53), opens `httpx.AsyncClient(follow_redirects=True, timeout=_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)` with no `event_hooks`, no custom `max_redirects` restriction, and no transport override. A repo-wide grep for `follow_redirects|event_hooks|max_redirects|on_redirect` confirms there is no shared client/transport wrapper anywhere in the codebase (security_assessment/base.py has zero references to httpx/transport/redirect) that would re-validate a redirect's destination before httpx transparently follows it.

Cross-checked the call chain in core/security_assessment.py: `assert_globally_routable_target` is invoked exactly once, in `_validate_scope` (line 301), which runs inside `start_run` before the background task is spawned. `_execute_run` (line 379) then calls `tool.run(target, ioc_type, profile_id)` directly (line 402) — the original `target` string, not a re-validated one, and no re-check occurs after that point. url_safety.py's own docstring for `assert_globally_routable_target` explicitly states this function exists because a value like `http://opensearch:9200/_cluster/health` was previously resolved to a real internal container IP and its response returned to the analyst as if external — i.e., exactly the SSRF class this finding says is reopened via a redirect hop instead of the initial hostname. Since the toolkit's targets are adversarial by definition (malicious IOCs under investigation), a target's own server returning a 30x to an internal address (docker-internal service name, 169.254.169.254, etc.) is a realistic and directly relevant threat model for this specific tool, not a generic hypothetical.

This is not covered by any of the eight listed intentional-design exceptions.

On severity: real-world impact is bounded by what the tool actually surfaces — only response headers, HTTP status, and the final `checked_url` (not the response body), and the result is shown to the investigating analyst rather than exfiltrated back to the external attacker. So this isn't a direct credential-exfiltration primitive as currently implemented, but it is a genuine bypass of a security control this codebase already treated as important enough to build and document (the exact 'opensearch:9200' incident), and it enables internal-network reconnaissance/fingerprinting via an authoritative security tool. That impact profile matches P1 (serious, exploitable, but not an immediate full-compromise P0) — the original reviewer's severity rating is reasonable and I'm not adjusting it.

title: assert_globally_routable_target's DNS resolution is a point-in-time check; every consuming tool re-resolves the same hostname independently at connect time (TOCTOU/DNS-rebinding)
actual_behavior: assert_globally_routable_target resolves the target hostname once (via socket.getaddrinfo) inside the synchronous API request handler, before the run row is even created. The resolved address is never passed down to the tool -- nmap_tool.py hands the ORIGINAL hostname string to the nmap subprocess (which performs its own DNS resolution), tls_tool.py calls socket.create_connection(host, port) with the original hostname (its own resolution), and http_headers_tool.py lets httpx resolve the same hostname again at connection time. The actual tool execution can happen well after the check (queued behind the 4-slot _scan_semaphore, or just ordinary async scheduling), and it re-resolves DNS from scratch.
failure_scenario: The target under investigation is a domain the analyst does not control, and by this feature's own threat model is expected to potentially be malicious infrastructure -- meaning its operator controls its own authoritative DNS. A low-TTL DNS record that returns a public IP on the validation-time query and a private/internal address (e.g. an internal docker-compose service, or a cloud metadata IP) on the later connect-time query defeats assert_globally_routable_target entirely: the check passes, but the actual nmap/TLS/HTTP connection goes to the rebound private address. This is the standard 'DNS rebinding' SSRF technique, and nothing here pins or re-validates the resolved address between check-time and connect-time.
proposed_fix: Resolve once in assert_globally_routable_target, pass the validated IP address down to each tool, and have each tool connect to that pinned IP (setting the original hostname only as TLS SNI / HTTP Host header) rather than letting each tool re-resolve DNS independently.

verdict.reasoning:
All the concrete technical claims check out against the actual code.

1. `assert_globally_routable_target` (url_safety.py:100-107) does a single `socket.getaddrinfo(host, None)` call, checks the resolved addresses with `ip.is_global`, then returns nothing — it discards the resolved IPs entirely and only validated the hostname string.

2. In `core/security_assessment.py`, this check runs inside `_validate_scope`, called synchronously at the top of `start_run` (line 320) — before the `SecurityAssessmentRun` row is even created (line 347) and before `_spawn_background` schedules `_execute_run` as an async task (line 372). `_execute_run` later does `async with _scan_semaphore:` (a real `asyncio.Semaphore(4)`, confirmed at lines 73-74) and then calls `await tool.run(target, ioc_type, profile_id)` (line 402) — passing the original hostname string, never a resolved/pinned address.

3. Each tool independently re-resolves that same hostname at actual connect time:
   - `nmap_tool.py` line 159: `argv = ["nmap", ..., target]` — nmap does its own internal DNS resolution of the raw hostname argv element.
   - `tls_tool.py` line 57: `socket.create_connection((host, port), ...)` inside `_connect_sync`, where `host` is the original target string (from `_host_and_port`, which just parses the URL, no resolution/pinning) — a fresh OS-level resolution.
   - `http_headers_tool.py` line 49: `await client.get(url)` via `httpx.AsyncClient()` with `url` built directly from `target` — httpx resolves DNS itself at connect time.

This is a textbook DNS-rebinding TOCTOU: the check-time resolution and each tool's connect-time resolution are two independent DNS queries, separated by a real, non-trivial time gap (DB commit, audit log, semaphore queueing behind up to 4 concurrent scans). A malicious/low-TTL authoritative DNS answer (the exact threat model this module's own docstring describes — "targets are threat-intel IOCs... never this application's own infrastructure") can trivially return a public IP for the validation query and a private/internal address for the later connect, defeating the control this file explicitly exists to enforce (its own docstring cites a real prior SSRF into the `opensearch` container as the motivating incident). No IP pinning, SNI-only-hostname pattern, or re-validation at connect time exists anywhere in these three tool files.

Severity: the original P2 undersells this. It doesn't just weaken a defense — it comprehensively defeats the control for precisely the adversary this feature's own docstrings say to expect (a domain operator who is potentially malicious infrastructure and therefore controls their own authoritative DNS), using a well-known, tooling-supported technique (DNS rebinding), and it affects all three network-touching tools (nmap, TLS, HTTP headers), enabling the backend to be forced into scanning/connecting to arbitrary internal targets (other containers, cloud metadata, etc.) with results surfaced in assessment findings. That's a real internal-SSRF/network-reconnaissance impact, not a theoretical one — I'm raising it to P1. It's not P0 because it doesn't hand the external attacker the response data directly (only the investigating team sees findings) and doesn't by itself achieve credential theft (e.g., http_headers_tool only inspects headers, not body content), which is why I stopped short of P0.

title: max_runtime_minutes and max_requests are accepted, persisted, and displayed but never enforced anywhere; expires_at/EXPIRED are dead code
actual_behavior: CreateAssessmentRequest accepts max_runtime_minutes/max_requests, PentestAssessment persists them and started_at, and the API/UI display them as if they bound execution. _run_assessment() tracks a local `request_count` (line 381, incremented at line 447) but never compares it against assessment.max_requests anywhere. There is no comparison of elapsed time (now - started_at) against max_runtime_minutes anywhere in _run_assessment() or _assessment_should_halt(). `expires_at` (models/pentest.py line 94) is never assigned a value anywhere in the codebase (grep confirms zero write sites) -- it is always None. PentestAssessmentStatus.EXPIRED is referenced defensively in several guard conditions (e.g. _assessment_should_halt line 372-373, exploit.py line 296) but no code path ever transitions an assessment INTO that status -- it is unreachable dead state.
failure_scenario: An operator creates an assessment with max_runtime_minutes=5 and max_requests=10 expecting the platform to self-limit a long-running scan against a live third-party-adjacent network. With many targets/tools queued, the orchestrator will keep running (and keep sending real network probes) for as long as it takes to work through every target/tool, with no automatic stop at 5 minutes or 10 requests -- the only way to actually stop it is a human manually clicking Pause/Cancel/Emergency-Stop or the admin engaging the global kill switch. The declared safety bound is purely cosmetic.
proposed_fix: In _assessment_should_halt() (or the per-target/per-phase checkpoints in _run_assessment()), also compare `datetime.now(timezone.utc) - assessment.started_at` against `assessment.max_runtime_minutes` and the running request_count against `assessment.max_requests`, transitioning to EXPIRED (or CANCELLED) and halting when either is exceeded.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of backend/app/pentest/orchestrator.py, backend/app/schemas/pentest.py, backend/app/models/pentest.py, and a repo-wide grep.

- schemas/pentest.py: CreateAssessmentRequest takes max_runtime_minutes (1-1440) and max_requests (1-100000) as real, bounded fields; AssessmentResponse echoes max_runtime_minutes, max_requests, started_at, and expires_at back to the caller for display -- all framed as if they bound execution.
- orchestrator.py start_assessment() (lines 333-362) sets started_at and status=ACTIVE, then spawns _run_assessment() as a background task.
- _run_assessment() (377-504) tracks a purely local `request_count` (381, incremented 447) that is never compared to assessment.max_requests anywhere, and never reads/compares `datetime.now(timezone.utc) - assessment.started_at` against assessment.max_runtime_minutes anywhere in the function.
- _assessment_should_halt() (365-374), the only halt-checkpoint function, checks only: the global kill switch, assessment.emergency_stopped, and assessment.status in (PAUSED, CANCELLED, EXPIRED). No time/request-count logic exists there either.
- Repo-wide grep for max_runtime_minutes/max_requests/expires_at/EXPIRED across backend/ shows expires_at (models/pentest.py:94) has zero write/assignment sites anywhere -- it's read-only in the API response mapper. EXPIRED is referenced only defensively as a guard condition (orchestrator.py:373, exploit.py:296, comments) and is never assigned to .status anywhere -- confirmed unreachable dead state.
- No separate scheduler/cron/watcher task exists anywhere in the backend (checked main.py and grepped the whole tree) that could be enforcing these limits out-of-band.

This exactly matches the claimed behavior: the declared safety bound is cosmetic. An operator who sets a tight max_runtime_minutes/max_requests expecting the platform to self-limit a live scan gets no such protection -- the only stops are manual (pause/cancel/emergency-stop) or the global admin kill switch.

This does not match any of the listed known-intentional design patterns (it's not about role/JWT trust, provider status semantics, AI narration-only scoring, basket visibility, toolkit duplication, nmap flag restriction, or provider status codes).

Severity: I kept it at P1 rather than escalating to P0 or downgrading to P2. It's not P0 because it doesn't grant unauthorized access, bypass the exploit-validation gates, or escalate technical scan aggressiveness -- the per-loop-iteration scope re-check (_is_in_scope, lines 404-405) still holds, and nmap profiles remain conservative (per the codebase's documented safety boundary) regardless of this bug. But it's a real, currently-exploitable-by-inaction gap in a safety control that is explicitly surfaced to operators as an enforced boundary (accepted via API validation, persisted, and displayed in the UI) for a tool that sends real network probes against live, possibly third-party-adjacent targets -- exceeding an operator's declared/authorized time or request budget has real legal/scope-of-engagement consequences in a pentest context. That combination (a security-relevant declared control that silently does nothing) warrants P1, matching the original reviewer's assessment.
